## Overview

The Klallam, also known as the S'Klallam or Clallam, are a Coast Salish people Indigenous to the northern Olympic Peninsula. Their historical territory extended along the north coast of the Olympic Peninsula from the mouth of the Hoko River to Port Discovery Bay, with communities also across the Strait of Juan de Fuca on Vancouver Island. Today, Klallam communities include the Lower Elwha Klallam and Jamestown S'Klallam on the Olympic Peninsula, the Port Gamble S'Klallam on the Kitsap Peninsula, and the Scia'new First Nation at Becher Bay in British Columbia. Their language, nəxʷsƛ̕ay̕əmúcən, is a Salishan language closely related to the Northern Straits Salish dialects. Klallam culture is documented through canoe making, fishing, oral history, potlatches, and language-revitalization efforts.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

 Paul Kane’s 1847 description records that shell money remained valued and that shamanism was still practiced.

### Architecture

Klallam villages were mostly located along the coast, while others stood inland along rivers, inlets, or large lakes. The sources mention houses in connection with an oral history about hoisting a log onto a house and describe a fortified village inhabited by about 200 Klallam in 1847.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The Klallam used stone adzes, fire, and heated water in canoe construction. The sources also record European-manufactured tools and utensils, cultivated potato fields, and earlier use of clubs and bows. During early contact, trade goods included knives, buttons, and copper. No specifically named Klallam ceramic tradition or metalworking tradition is described.

### Jewelry & body adornment

 They state that shell money was still valued in 1847.

## Music & performance

 They do document storytelling and potlatches. Potlatches played a large role in determining social status, and in 1999 a lesson plan and guidebooks were developed to teach students the basics of Klallam through storytelling. The sources also identify Elaine Grinnell as a Klallam storyteller and basket and drum maker.

## Festivals & rituals

 They record that Klallam communities held potlatches, which played a large role in determining social status. The sources also state that shamanism and slavery were still practiced in 1847 and that potlatching continued in 1855. No detailed descriptions of birth, coming-of-age, wedding, or funeral rites are provided.

## Foodways

Klallam territory supplied food from its lands, rivers, marine waters, and beaches throughout the year. Their diet included large and small land game, sea fowl, shellfish, and fish, with fish identified as the most important food source. Salmon continued to have nutritional and spiritual importance in Klallam culture. Klallam people fished year round with traps, trolling, gillnets, spears, rakes, dip nets, and holes dug in the beach. Specific locations were associated with particular fishes at the appropriate time of year, and different implements and skills were used for successful catches. The sources also mention cultivated potatoes, duck netting, and the former importance of the fur trade. No named Klallam dishes, beverages, cooking methods, or dietary rules are documented.

## Oral tradition & literature

Klallam oral history explains the name nəxʷsƛ̕áy̕əm̕, meaning “strong people.” According to the account, the name was earned after the tribe won a challenge involving the lifting of a log onto a house: the Klallam placed the log in water and floated it onto their shoulders, after which other tribes cheered “strong people.” The sources also describe storytelling as a method of teaching the language. In 1999, a lesson plan and guidebooks were developed to teach students the basics of Klallam through storytelling. No Klallam epic, proverb collection, riddle tradition, or written literary canon is identified.

## Language & religion

Klallam, also known as Clallam, Ns'Klallam, or S'klallam, is a Salishan language historically spoken at Beecher Bay on Vancouver Island and across the Strait of Juan de Fuca on the north coast of the Olympic Peninsula. It is closely related to the Northern Straits Salish dialects, including Sooke, Lekwungen, Saanich, Lummi, and Samish, although these languages are not mutually intelligible. Recorded dialects include Elwha Klallam, Becher Bay Klallam, Jamestown S'Klallam, and Little Boston S'Klallam. The last native speaker of Klallam as a first language, Hazel Sampson of Port Angeles, died on February 4, 2014, at the age of 103. A first Klallam dictionary was published in 2012, a complete grammar in 2015, and Klallam classes and immersion programs have continued in schools and at Peninsula College. The sources mention shamanism.
